passage: Late evening, text messages. Usha: Bhaiya, Amma just said everything is settled. Engagement in two weeks. They only need my nod. Shankar: Do you want it? Usha: I have met him for twenty minutes. I don't even know where we would live. Shankar: Then you're allowed to ask for more time. And for answers. Usha: What if Amma is hurt? She has already told the aunts. Shankar: Then she's hurt for a week. You saying yes out of fear is worse for both of you. Usha: And if my answer is no? Shankar: Then it's no. I'll tell Papa and Amma myself that nobody gets punished for it. Usha: Will you come when I ask for two more meetings? Shankar: I'll be sitting right next to you.

passage: After the paddy was stacked, Bhupen's father called the family into the courtyard of their village home near Jorhat. "Everything is fixed with Vandana's people," he said, beaming. "The date is in Magh. Only your nod is needed." Bhupen's mother passed round the betel-nut without looking up. Bhupen, twenty-five, had spoken to Vandana once, at a cousin's wedding, for a few minutes. His throat felt dry. "Baba, I'd like a fortnight. I want to meet her and her father, with my sister there, before I say anything." His father's smile went stiff. "Asking is not an insult," Bhupen's mother said quietly. Days later, on her veranda, Vandana told him she too had been told only a nod was needed. "I'm glad you asked," she said. "Ask me anything, and know that I can say no too."

So, Shalini, you asked about the day of the ring. Okay.
I came home from work and there were sweets on the table and my father's cousins in the living room. Mummy pulled me into the kitchen. "Rukmini beti, everything is fixed. Good family, they've seen your photo, you only have to say yes." I asked, "Fixed when?" She said, "Last Sunday."
I had met him once. For twenty minutes.
I remember my hands were cold. I remember thinking, if I say no now, in front of everyone, what happens to me in this house?
I said, "I need two weeks and three more meetings." My mother cried. My father didn't speak to me for four days.
Those two weeks, I learned he wanted me to leave my job. So I said no. It cost me. But it was the first real choice anyone had let me make. That's my story, Shalini, and I'm Rukmini, and I'm still here.

qa.a: Rukmini had met him once, for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when her hands were cold?
qa.a: Rukmini felt frightened and trapped, wondering what would happen to her in the house if she refused in front of everyone.

qa.q: What could Rukmini's parents have done to make her consent real?
qa.a: They could have given her time and more meetings before fixing anything, shared full information about the match, and promised she could refuse without anger or silence.

qa.q: What is it like for Shalini, as host, to hear this story?
qa.a: Shalini hears how a nod was expected without real choice, and may feel moved by what it cost Rukmini to ask for time and say no.

Wednesday. Hansa's Bade Papa came with the news: "It's settled with the Mehta family. They're happy. Only your yes is needed." Hansa, twenty-four, said nothing through dinner. Imran, the neighbours' son who had grown up in and out of their house, watched her push rice around her plate.
Saturday. Imran knocked on her door. "Do you want this?" Hansa whispered, "I don't know him. And if I say no, Bade Papa will say I shamed him." Imran said, "Then we ask for time together. I'll sit beside you."
The next Tuesday. In the living room, Hansa said, "I'm not saying no. I'm asking for three months, two meetings a month, and his answers about my work." Bade Papa frowned. Imran said, "It's her whole life." Slowly, Bade Papa nodded. "Three months."

qa.q: How long did Hansa ask for?
qa.a: Hansa asked for three months, two meetings a month, and his answers about her work.

qa.q: What was Hansa afraid of when she whispered to Imran?
qa.a: She was afraid that if she said no, Bade Papa would say she had shamed him, so she felt trapped between the family's plan and her own doubts.

qa.q: How did Imran support Hansa in a helpful way?
qa.a: He asked what she wanted, suggested asking for time together, and sat beside her so she was not alone when she spoke to the family.

qa.q: How might Bade Papa see the request for three months?
qa.a: He may first feel it delays a settled plan and risks his word to the Mehta family, but he agrees, perhaps seeing that a real yes needs time.

grounding: It shows across three days a young woman told a match is settled and only her nod is needed, and how time and a safe way to refuse make consent real.

You're asking why I never pushed you toward anyone, Nandini? Let me tell you about 1979.
I was twenty-five, working in the railway office. One evening your great-grandfather said, "The girl's family has agreed. The date is in April. You'll meet her at the engagement." That was all. My consent was a formality, a nod.
I didn't nod. I asked to meet her first. My father was furious; he said I was humiliating him. But I went to her home with my aunt, and the girl, Roshan, told me quietly that she had wanted to study nursing and nobody had asked her either.
We both said no that week. Both families shouted for a month. And then it passed.
Roshan became a nurse. I married your grandmother three years later, after we'd talked for a year. So that's why, Nandini. A nod isn't a yes. This is Zubin Mama telling you so.

qa.q: What had Roshan wanted to study?
qa.a: Roshan had wanted to study nursing.

qa.q: How did Roshan probably feel when she told Zubin quietly that nobody had asked her either?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved to be asked at last, and hopeful that she could still refuse and follow her plan to study nursing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Zubin's story?
qa.a: The turning point was when he refused to simply nod and asked to meet Roshan first, which let both of them say what they wanted.

qa.q: How might Roshan's family have felt during that month of shouting?
qa.a: Roshan's family were probably angry and embarrassed that the settled match had fallen through, before the upset slowly passed.

grounding: An elder recalls being told a match was settled and only his nod was needed, and how he and the young woman both needed time and a safe way to refuse.

The engagement guests were due at six, and it was already half past four. Parul, twenty-four, sat on her bed in a new saree she hadn't chosen while her mother pinned flowers in her hair. "Everything is settled, beta. The boy's family is good. You only have to nod." Parul had met him once, for twenty minutes, with six relatives in the room. She didn't know if he wanted children, where they'd live, or whether she could keep her job. Her throat felt shut.
Chandrika masi came in with the tea tray, saw Parul's face and asked her mother to check the kitchen. She shut the door. "Tell me honestly. Do you want this?" Parul whispered, "I don't know him." Masi nodded. "Then you need time. And if the answer is no, no one in this house will punish you. I'll make sure." She went out and told Parul's parents the ceremony would wait.

qa.q: What time were the engagement guests due?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: How did Parul feel being told she only had to nod?
qa.a: She felt trapped and frightened, her throat shut, because she barely knew the man and nothing had been asked of her.

qa.q: What did Chandrika masi do that made real consent possible?
qa.a: She asked Parul privately, promised she would not be punished for saying no, and got the family to wait so Parul could have time and information.

qa.q: How might Parul's mother have felt when the ceremony was delayed?
qa.a: She was probably shocked and anxious about the guests, though she believed she was doing her best for Parul.

grounding: It illustrates a young woman told everything is settled and only her nod is needed, and how time, information and a safe way to refuse make consent real.
